data.heading: Three reasons people wait, and what the book says to each.

cards.title: “AI is overhyped.”
cards.line: The Mirror Principle: AI reflects the quality of your direction (Ch 1).
cards.body: The model has no goals of its own, so it mirrors back what you bring. The book's image is a lamp against a beam: a vague prompt lights the whole room, and a precise one narrows the beam onto the thing you need. A flat answer usually tells you the brief was thin, and a brief can be fixed.

cards.title: “I'm not technical.”
cards.line: The skill is direction, and you already use it at work (Ch 3).
cards.body:
The Director's Mindset puts you in the chair with AI as the crew. You supply the judgment, the direction and the check, which is what you already do when you hand work to a colleague.

Priya, a consultant in the book (a character, a composite), practised for two weeks in January and had twelve templates by March, and “no technical training went into any of it.”

cards.title: “The tools change too fast.”
cards.line: A good brief carries over from one model to the next (Ch 6).
cards.body: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini share the same engine underneath, and each one mirrors the quality of what you type. In the book's words, “The skill you're building here transfers to every tool, because the underlying engine is the same one.” Product names will keep changing, and your briefs keep working.

data.intro: The book follows three characters whose starting points may look like yours.

cast.name: Maya
cast.line: A high-school English teacher who doubted AI on principle (Ch 2).
cast.body: After eleven years in the classroom, she tested AI on her own work first, on a task that reliably took forty minutes. Six months later she still reads every output before it reaches her students. What changed was her question, from whether to use it at all to whether she has checked it.

cast.name: Priya
cast.line: A consultant with more client work than hours (Ch 5).
cast.body: She gave herself two weeks in January to draft every client brief with AI first. By March she had twelve templates. Within a few months those workflows had clawed back close to two days a week, and she put that time into a fourth client account.

cast.name: Marcus
cast.line: A launch manager who closed the tab after one bad answer (Ch 3).
cast.body: His story runs through the whole book. It's told in the next section.

data.heading: Your first week, then your first three months.
data.intro: Chapter 14 turns what you read into a practice plan.

steps.title: One real task a day, with low stakes.
steps.body: Each workday, use AI for one task that needs doing anyway: an email, a summary, an outline or some research for a decision. Keep the stakes low enough that a mistake costs nothing. Save the first prompt that works (Ch 5 shows you how).

steps.title: Reaching for AI becomes your default.
steps.body: Keep one real task a day. At the end of each week, find one task you did more than once and save a template for it. You'll know it's working when you stop asking whether to use AI for something and just use it.

steps.title: You can say why a good output was good.
steps.body: Sharpen the templates that needed fixing every time. Try ranking the details that matter most and putting them first. On one complex task, ask AI to interview you before it answers.

steps.title: Your prompt library becomes part of how you work.
steps.body: Organise your library by task, workflow or audience. The book pictures a Tuesday at week twelve where a request that once ate your afternoon becomes a strong draft twenty minutes later.

data.heading: AI can sound certain and still be wrong. Two steps catch it.
data.intro: A story from Chapter 13 about two colleagues and one confident number.

panels.label: 1 · Same prompt
panels.text: Diana and James asked AI for a market size for the same client pitch. It came back confident, with a growth rate to the decimal.

panels.label: 2 · James
panels.text: He pasted the number into his slide and moved on. It looked right and read right.

panels.label: 3 · Diana
panels.text: She paused and checked where the figure came from before it went on a slide.

panels.label: 4 · The meeting
panels.text: The client flagged James's number as outdated. He spent fifteen minutes explaining. Diana spent thirty seconds citing her source.

data.note: Diana and James are characters from the book, composites.

cards.title: Sort the claim
cards.line: Is it a fact, a judgment call or a creative draft?
cards.body: Facts can be flatly right or wrong, so that's where your checking goes. Judgment calls get your own judgment, and drafts get judged on fit.

cards.title: Match effort to stakes
cards.line: A glance for small things, and an expert for big ones.
cards.body: A book suggestion gets a quick look. A figure going in front of a client gets a real check. Legal, financial or medical claims go to a professional.

data.heading: Waiting has a cost, and the book calls it the Foundation Tax.
data.quote: “The most expensive time to learn something is right after you needed it.”
data.chart_label: Two curves: starting early climbs gently, starting late climbs steeply after the skill is already expected

cards.title: What the tax is
cards.line: The extra cost of learning a skill after it's expected (Ch 5).
cards.body: The book defines it as “the extra cost, in time, energy, and credibility, that deferred learning charges when the environment already assumes a fluency you haven't built.” It builds slowly and then shows up all at once.

cards.title: What two early weeks bought
cards.line: Priya's head start came from her calendar (Ch 5, a character from the book).
cards.body: She practised for two weeks in January while the learning curve was forgiving. Within a few months she had close to two days a week back. The book's advice is to start while free tiers and patient teams still make practice cheap.

data.heading: Questions people ask before they buy

items.q: Do I need a technical background?
items.a: None. The book is written for professionals with no technical training. If you can write an email, you can use everything in it.

items.q: Which AI tool does it use?
items.a: It works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot. Part 2 helps you pick one, and the directing skill carries over to all of them.

items.q: Will it go out of date when the tools change?
items.a: The book teaches you how to direct AI, and that skill carries over from one model to the next. The product names will keep changing, and your briefs will keep working.

items.q: I already use AI at work. Is it still for me?
items.a: Yes, if your results are hit and miss. The frameworks turn scattered habits into a method you can repeat, and the appendices give you prompts and fixes to keep beside your work.

items.q: What if AI gets something wrong?
items.a: Chapter 13 gives you a two-step check: sort the claim, then match your checking to the stakes. Appendix F covers invented facts and nine other common failures, each with a corrective prompt.

items.q: I'm a manager. Can my team use it?
items.a: Yes. Chapter 7 helps a team settle on one tool, and the saved-template habit gives everyone prompts to share. One copy per person keeps the whole team on the same method.

items.q: Can I read some of it first?
items.a: Yes. Chapter 8 is free to read, and it shows you which AI mode fits which job.
